'''Trevor Henry Worthy''' (born 3 January 1957) is an Australia-based paleozoologist from New Zealand, [[Knowledge|known]] for his [[research]] on [[moa]] and other [[Extinction|extinct]] [[Vertebrate|vertebrates]].

==Biography==
Worthy grew up in [[Broadwood, New Zealand|Broadwood]], [[Northland Region|Northland]], and went to [[Whangarei Boys' High School]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url = http://www.waikato.ac.nz/news-events/media/2011/mr-moa-now-doctor-of-science|title = Mr Moa now Doctor of Science|date = 29 April 2011|access-date = 7 February 2016|website = News at Waikato|publisher = University of Waikato|last = |first = }}</ref> He began his career as a largely self-taught palaeontologist, after becoming interested in fossils through caving.<ref name="NZ_Herald_10124525">{{cite news |url=http://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=10124525 |title=Mr Moa's cash extinct |author=Beston, Anne |date=9 May 2005 |work=[[The New Zealand Herald]] |accessdate=24 November 2011}}</ref> Worthy completed his [[BSc]] and [[MSc]] at the [[University of Waikato]], then did a second Master's degree at [[Victoria University of Wellington]].<ref name=":0" />

In 1987, Worthy described three new [[Leiopelmatidae|leiopelmatid]] frog species from cave subfossils: the Aurora frog (''[[Leiopelma auroraensis]]''), [[Markham's frog]] (''Leiopelma markhami''), and the [[Waitomo frog]] (''Leiopelma waitomoensis''). In the 1990s, he discovered several fossil bird species new to science, including the [[Long-billed wren (New Zealand)|long-billed wren]] (''Dendroscansor decurvirostris'') in 1991, [[Scarlett's shearwater]] (''Puffinus spelaeus'') in 1991, and the [[Niue night heron]] (''Nycticorax kalavikai'') in 1995. In 1991, he also described the [[Northland skink]], a fossil skink species new to science.<ref name="Ecology Nov 2009">{{cite journal|last1=Tennyson|first1=Alan J.D.|title=The origin and history of New Zealand's terrestrial vertebrates|journal=New Zealand Journal of Ecology|date=4 November 2009|issue=Special Issue: Feathers to Fur|page=9|url=http://newzealandecology.org/nzje/2914.pdf|accessdate=18 July 2015}}</ref>

In 1998, Worthy excavated subfossil bones in [[Fiji]], where he found remains of the flightless [[Viti Levu giant pigeon]] (''Natunaornis gigoura''), the [[Viti Levu scrubfowl]] (''Megapodius amissus''), the [[Viti Levu snipe]] (''Coenocorypha miratropica''), the [[giant Fiji ground frog]] (''Platymantis megabotoniviti''), and the small freshwater crocodile ''[[Volia|Volia athollandersoni]]''. The holotypes of these species were deposited in the [[Museum of New Zealand Te Papa Tongarewa]].

For years, Worthy has been involved in the excavation of Miocene fossils (the [[Saint Bathans Fauna]]) from a prehistoric lake in [[Central Otago]], including the oldest known moa bones, the oldest [[tuatara]] bones, and the first known fossil land mammal from New Zealand.<ref>"[https://www.newscientist.com/article/dn10773-fossils-reveal-new-zealands-indigenous-mouse.html Fossils reveal New Zealand's indigenous 'mouse']". ''New Scientist''. 11 December 2006.</ref>

Worthy's research, based in [[Waitomo Caves]], [[Masterton]], [[Nelson, New Zealand|Nelson]], and [[Museum of New Zealand Te Papa Tongarewa|Te Papa]], had been funded by grants from the [[Foundation for Research, Science and Technology]] since 1991, but in 2005 his funding was cut by the Foundation.<ref name="NZ_Herald_10124525" /> From 2005 to 2009, he was at the [[University of Adelaide]], where he received his [[PhD]] in 2008. He received a [[Doctor of Science]] from the University of Waikato in 2011.<ref name=":0" /> He was at the [[University of New South Wales]] from 2009 to 2011, back at the University of Adelaide during 2012, and has been at [[Flinders University]] since 2013. In May 2019, he ended his 30-year research association with Te Papa at protest to the [[Museum_of_New_Zealand_Te_Papa_Tongarewa#Te_Papa|staff restructuring controversy]].<ref name="stuff-19-10">{{cite web|url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/science/112905562/mr-moa-scientist-cuts-30year-te-papa-connection-over-staff-treatment|title=Mr Moa scientist cuts 30-year Te Papa connection over staff treatment|publisher=Stuff.co.nz|accessdate=11 April 2019}}</ref>

Worthy is author or co-author of numerous research papers about prehistoric life in New Zealand. For the book ''The Lost World of the Moa'' (2002), he and Richard Holdaway received the [[D. L. Serventy Medal]] from the [[Royal Australasian Ornithologists Union]] in 2003 for an outstanding published work about [[Australasia]]n [[Bird|avifauna]].
